## Intuition

The **Feynman-Kac Formula** establishes a link between
[[calculus|Parabolic PDEs]] and
[[probability-theory|stochastic processes]].
It offers a method of solving certain PDEs by simulating random paths of a
stochastic process. Conversely, an important class of expectations of random
processes can be computed by deterministic methods.

:::{.intuition data-title="Averaging over random paths"}

Think of the PDE as describing how a quantity $u$ is *transported and
smoothed* backwards in time from the terminal value $\psi$. The drift
$\mu$ moves information along, and the diffusion $\sigma$ blurs it, exactly as
in the [[heat-equation]]. Instead of solving for $u$ everywhere at once, we
can release a particle at $x$ at time $t$, let it wander according to the
[[ito-process]] $X$, and *average* what it collects along the way:

- $\psi(X_T)$ is the payoff it collects at the end,
- $f(X_s,s)$ is a reward collected continuously along the path,
- $V(X_s,s)$ is a rate at which the collected amount is discounted (or the
  particle is "killed").

The average of all of this over many paths is $u(x,t)$.

:::

## Feynman-Kac Formula

:::{.theorem data-title="Feynman-Kac Formula"}

Consider the PDE

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_{t}(x,t) & +\mu(x,t)u_{x}(x,t)+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(x,t)u_{xx}(x,t) \\
& -V(x,t)u(x,t)+f(x,t)=0,
\end{aligned}
$$

defined for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $t \in [0,T]$ subject to the terminal
condition
$$
u(x,T)=\psi (x),
$$
where $\mu,\sigma,\psi,V,f$ are known functions, $T$ is a parameter, and
$u:\mathbb{R}\times[0,T]\to \mathbb{R}$ is the unknown. The Feynman-Kac
formula expresses $u(x,t)$ as a conditional expectation under a probability
measure $\mathbb{Q}$
$$
u(x,t)=\mathbb{E}^\mathbb{Q}\left[
e^{-\int_{t}^{T}V(X_{r},r)\,dr}\,\psi(X_{T})
+\int_{t}^{T}e^{-\int_{t}^{s}V(X_{r},r)\,dr}f(X_{s},s)\,ds
\,\middle|\, X_{t}=x \right],
$$
where $X$ is an [[ito-process]] satisfying
$$
dX_{s}=\mu(X_{s},s)ds+\sigma(X_{s},s)dW_{s}^\mathbb{Q},
$$
and $W^\mathbb{Q}$ is [[brownian-motion]] under $\mathbb{Q}$.

:::

*Remark.* The operator
$\mathcal{L}u=\mu u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2u_{xx}$ appearing in the PDE is the
[[infinitesimal-generator]] of $X$, so the PDE can be written compactly as
$u_{t}+\mathcal{L}u-Vu+f=0$. The formula says that the solution of this
backward equation is an expectation over the diffusion with that generator.

The statement is valid under standard regularity conditions (e.g. $\mu,\sigma$
Lipschitz with linear growth, $u$ of class $C^{1,2}$ and
$\mathbb{E}\int_t^T\sigma^2u_x^2\,ds<\infty$ so that the stochastic integral
below is a true martingale).

:::{.proof}

Fix $(x,t)$ and write $A_{s}=\int_{t}^{s}V(X_{r},r)\,dr$, so that
$dA_{s}=V(X_{s},s)ds$. Apply the [[ito-formula]] to the process
$e^{-A_{s}}u(X_{s},s)$ for $s\in[t,T]$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
d\left(e^{-A_{s}}u(X_{s},s)\right)
& = e^{-A_{s}}\left(u_{t}+\mu u_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2u_{xx}-Vu\right)ds
+e^{-A_{s}}\sigma u_{x}\,dW_{s}^\mathbb{Q}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The PDE says the bracket equals $-f(X_{s},s)$, so
$$
d\left(e^{-A_{s}}u(X_{s},s)\right)
=-e^{-A_{s}}f(X_{s},s)\,ds+e^{-A_{s}}\sigma u_{x}\,dW_{s}^\mathbb{Q}.
$$
Integrating from $t$ to $T$, using $A_{t}=0$, $X_{t}=x$ and $u(X_{T},T)=\psi(X_{T})$,
$$
e^{-A_{T}}\psi(X_{T})-u(x,t)
=-\int_{t}^{T}e^{-A_{s}}f(X_{s},s)\,ds
+\int_{t}^{T}e^{-A_{s}}\sigma u_{x}\,dW_{s}^\mathbb{Q}.
$$
Take $\mathbb{E}^\mathbb{Q}[\,\cdot\mid X_{t}=x]$. The Itô integral is a
martingale started at zero, so its expectation vanishes, and rearranging gives
$$
u(x,t)=\mathbb{E}^\mathbb{Q}\left[e^{-A_{T}}\psi(X_{T})
+\int_{t}^{T}e^{-A_{s}}f(X_{s},s)\,ds\,\middle|\,X_{t}=x\right],
$$
which is the claim, since $e^{-A_{s}}=e^{-\int_{t}^{s}V(X_{r},r)dr}$.
:::

In other words, the process
$$
M_{s}=e^{-A_{s}}u(X_{s},s)+\int_{t}^{s}e^{-A_{r}}f(X_{r},r)\,dr
$$
is a [[martingale-theory|martingale]], and the formula is just
$\mathbb{E}[M_{T}]=M_{t}$. The proof only shows that a smooth solution *must*
have this form (uniqueness); existence of a smooth solution needs extra
conditions on the coefficients.

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="Heat equation"}

Take $X=W$ (so $\mu=0$, $\sigma=1$), $V=f=0$ and $\psi(x)=x^2$. The PDE is
the backward [[heat-equation]]
$$
u_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}u_{xx}=0,\qquad u(x,T)=x^2.
$$
The formula gives
$$
u(x,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[W_{T}^2\mid W_{t}=x\right]
=x^2+(T-t),
$$
since $W_{T}=x+(W_{T}-W_{t})$ with $W_{T}-W_{t}\sim N(0,T-t)$. Check:
$u_{t}=-1$ and $\tfrac{1}{2}u_{xx}=1$, so the PDE holds.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Running reward"}

Take $X=W$, $V=0$, $\psi=0$ and $f=1$. Then
$$
u(x,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{t}^{T}1\,ds\right]=T-t,
$$
which indeed solves $u_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}u_{xx}+1=0$ with $u(x,T)=0$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Discounting"}

Take $X=W$, $f=0$, $\psi=1$ and constant $V=\lambda$. The formula gives
$u(x,t)=e^{-\lambda(T-t)}$, which solves
$u_{t}+\tfrac{1}{2}u_{xx}-\lambda u=0$. The term $V$ is a pure discount (or
killing) rate.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Black-Scholes"}

Let $X=S$ follow a [[geometric-brownian-motion]] under the
[[risk-neutral-measure]], $dS=rS\,dt+\sigma S\,dW^\mathbb{Q}$, with $V=r$ and
$f=0$. The PDE becomes
$$
u_{t}+rxu_{x}+\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2x^2u_{xx}-ru=0,\qquad u(x,T)=\psi(x),
$$
which is the [[black-scholes-pde-bspde|Black-Scholes PDE]], and the formula
reads
$$
u(S_{t},t)=e^{-r(T-t)}\,\mathbb{E}^\mathbb{Q}\left[\psi(S_{T})\mid S_{t}\right],
$$
the familiar statement that an option price is the discounted risk-neutral
expectation of its payoff. For a call, $\psi(x)=(x-K)^+$.

:::

## Where it is used

- **Financial mathematics.** The link between the
  [[black-scholes-merton-model]] PDE and risk-neutral pricing, and its
  extensions to stochastic volatility, interest rate and barrier models
  ([[barrier-options]]). Here $V$ is the short rate and $f$ a dividend or
  coupon stream.
- **Numerical methods.** In high dimensions, grid-based PDE solvers fail
  (curse of dimensionality) but the expectation can be estimated by Monte
  Carlo: simulate paths of $X$ ([[sde-simulation]]) and average the payoff.
  Conversely, low-dimensional expectations can be computed by a PDE solver.
- **Quantum mechanics.** With $\mu=0$ and $\sigma^2=\hbar/m$ (and imaginary
  time) the PDE is the [[schrodinger-equation]] with potential $V$; the
  formula is the Feynman path integral made rigorous by Kac, hence the name.
- **Probability and PDE theory.** Probabilistic representations of solutions
  to PDEs (e.g. the [[diffusion-equation]]), killing rates and survival
  probabilities, and links to the backward
  [[kolmogorov-equations]] and the [[fokker-planck-equation]].
- **Stochastic control.** The same argument applied to a controlled process
  leads to the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation ([[stochastic-control]]).
